Because further processing in Mexico did not satisfy the section 102.20 tariff shift for heading 3926, the Chinese components decided the country of origin under 19 CFR Part 102, retaining China as the country of origin.

Under ruling N331595, CBP held that the metallized PET film originated in China because under 19 CFR 102.11(b), the metallized PET film produced in China was the single material that imparted the essential character to the finished good (as it was classified in a tariff provision from which a change was not allowed under Section 102.20).

Ruling H285605 concerns the country of origin of a buried splice kit classified as a set under GRI 3(b) and evaluated under 19 CFR 102.11(c). The operations in the ruling consist merely of packaging foreign components together in Mexico. None of the components or processes involve extruding/metallizing PET film, forming polypropylene plastic foil, or scoring/pre-cutting divider bodies and tabs of heading 3926.

The ruling determines the origin of a shower system kit classified as a set under GRI 3 using 19 CFR 102.11(c), finding that components from Canada, Germany, and India merit equal consideration for essential character. The ruling does not mention PET film extrusion/metallization, cutting/scoring along kiss-cut fold lines, or pre-cutting divider bodies and tabs under heading 3926 as a tariff-shift or origin-deciding factor.

Ruling N330295 determined that polypropylene resin (heading 3902) from Taiwan underwent the requisite tariff shift in Mexico under 19 CFR 102.20 to become drinkware lids classified in heading 3923, thereby establishing Mexico as the country of origin under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).

In Ruling N331459, the artificial trees of heading 6702 are made wholly of plastic components in China. Under 19 CFR Part 102 (essential character analysis), CBP determined that the Chinese-origin artificial trees impart the essential character to the finished potted articles, making China the country of origin.

Ruling N306037 evaluated the 'PopLips PopGrip,' which incorporates a plastic collapsible grip made in China and lip balm made in the United States, packaged together in Mexico. Under 19 CFR 102.11(d)(1), CBP held the countries of origin to be China and the United States because packaging in Mexico was a simple operation and the essential character could not be determined under 102.11(b), making the manufacture of the grip in China directly decisive of origin as one of the component origins.

Under 19 CFR 102.11(c), CBP held that the country of origin of the buried splice kit is Belgium and the United States because the components meriting equal consideration for essential character included the isolated plastic cover (along with the bond bar and plastic mesh), which is a product of the United States.

Ruling N273778 concerns a shower system kit that includes a polystyrene plastic shower curb and shower base (ProVa Shower Curb and Shower Pan), which are Canadian components that merit equal consideration under 19 CFR 102.11(c) for determining essential character, leading CBP to hold Canada as one of the countries of origin.

Ruling N308174 addresses plastic dividers processed in Mexico by folding along pre-scored lines, heat-sealing edges and tabs, and punching holes. CBP found that both the unfinished Chinese sheets and the finished dividers were classified under subheading 3926.10, meaning the required tariff shift under 19 CFR 102.20 was not met, and held that the country of origin remained China rather than Mexico.

Ruling N308175 directly addresses folding pre-scored plastic divider sheets, heat-sealing edges and pockets, and punching binder holes in Mexico on Chinese-origin plastic pieces. Under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) and 102.20, CBP determined that this work failed to satisfy the required tariff shift for heading 3926 because both the incoming material and the finished product were classified under subheading 3926.10, resulting in the country of origin remaining China.

Ruling N331595 involved metallized PET film imported from China into Canada, where processing failed to achieve the required tariff shift under 19 CFR 102.20. Origin was determined under 19 CFR 102.11(b) by the essential character imparted by the Chinese film, confirming that the country where the work was done was not the country of origin.

Ruling N331459 addresses setting artificial plastic trees from China into ceramic pots with expanding foam, cardboard, artificial dirt, and moss in Mexico. Under 19 CFR Part 102, CBP held that Mexico was not the country of origin because the Chinese-origin artificial trees imparted the essential character to the finished goods, making China the country of origin for marking purposes.

Ruling N306037 evaluated the packaging of a Chinese plastic grip and US lip balm into retail packaging in Mexico. CBP determined that packaging the components did not effect the required tariff shift under 19 CFR 102.20 due to 19 CFR 102.17 (simple packaging), and ultimately determined under 19 CFR 102.11(d)(1) that Mexico was not the country of origin, holding instead that the origin was China and the United States.

Ruling N273778 concerns packaging components into a DIY retail kit (the ProVa Shower System) in Canada. CBP held that the kit did not qualify as originating in Canada alone based on the assembly/packaging work because not every foreign material underwent the required tariff shift under 19 CFR 102.20; applying 19 CFR 102.11(c) for sets, the countries of origin were determined by the components that merit equal consideration (Canada, Germany, and India).

Ruling N303599 held that the country of origin of the pushbutton stations was France because the pushbutton switches (heading 8536 / subheading 8536.50) were manufactured in France and determined origin pursuant to Section 102.11(d)(1).

In Ruling N330771, the finished busbar assemblies were classified under heading 8537, requiring a tariff shift from any other heading under 19 CFR 102.20. In Mexico, aluminum/copper sheets were stamped, punched, formed, deburred, milled, and nickel-plated into conductors, and assembled with Chinese flexible electrical connectors and insulating materials into the final assemblies. CBP held that because all foreign components were classified outside heading 8537, the required tariff shift occurred in Mexico, confirming Mexican origin under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).

In Ruling N301448, CBP determined that the country of origin of the finished goods (assembled in Mexico using Chinese copper conductors and multi-pin connectors of heading 8536) was Mexico, because the required tariff shift to heading 8537 was met under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3). The claim incorrectly asserts that the work did not make the country where the work was done the origin and that CBP held another country.

The claim asserts that using the operation group's output did not make the country where the work was done the origin. However, in Ruling N303603, CBP held that the country of origin of the electrical junction boxes assembled in Canada (using terminal blocks, cross connectors, etc.) was Canada, because the foreign components met the tariff shift under 19 CFR 102.20.

The claim states that the operation group's work or using its output did not make the country where the work was done the origin. However, in Ruling N303604, CBP held that Canada (where the assembly of the electrical junction box incorporating terminal blocks and cross connectors took place) WAS the country of origin under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) because the components satisfied the requisite tariff shift to heading 8537.

The claim states that the operation group's work did not make the country where the work was done the origin and that CBP held another country. However, in Ruling N303606, the assembly work was done in Canada and CBP ultimately held that the country of origin of the RIO panel is Canada (pursuant to 19 CFR 102.11(d)(3)).

The claim asserts that the work did not make the country where it was done the country of origin and that CBP held another country. However, in Ruling N301448, the assembly work was performed in Mexico and CBP held that the country of origin is Mexico because the foreign components underwent the required tariff shift under 19 CFR 102.20.

Ruling N303599 held that the country of origin of pushbutton stations assembled in Canada—using US-produced stainless or carbon steel enclosures (subheading 7326.90) and French pushbutton switches (subheading 8536.50)—was France under 19 CFR 102.11(d)(1) because the assembly did not meet the required tariff shift for foreign switches, meaning the enclosure work/incorporation did not confer origin to Canada.

In Ruling N303603, CBP held that the country of origin of the electrical junction boxes was Canada because the foreign components (including the enclosure from Germany) satisfied the required tariff shift under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3), directly contradicting the claim that the country where the work was done was not the country of origin.

The claim states that the operation did not make the country where the work was done the origin and that CBP held another country. In Ruling N303604, CBP explicitly held that the country of origin is Canada (the country where the assembly work was done) because the foreign components satisfied the requisite tariff shift.

The claim states that the operation group's work did not make the country where the work was done the origin and that CBP held another country. However, in Ruling N330771, the assembly and processing work occurred in Mexico, the foreign components met the tariff shift rule under 19 CFR 102.20, and CBP held that the country of origin was indeed Mexico, not another country.

Ruling N302344 held that the country of origin of transformer toroids (classified under subheading 8504.90) is Mexico. The ruling explicitly determined origin under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) because foreign silicon electrical steel of subheading 7225.11 was slit, cut, and wound in Mexico into toroids of subheading 8504.90, fulfilling the required tariff shift under Section 102.20 ('change to subheading 8504.90 from any other heading'). This matches the work described in the operation group.
The ruling held that the country of origin of the RIO panel was Canada (the country where the assembly occurred) under 19 CFR 102.11(d)(3), contradicting the claim that CBP held another country.

In ruling N301448, CBP determined that the country of origin of the bus bar assemblies (subheading 8537.10) is Mexico. The assembly of the conductors, adhesive strips, insulating bases, fasteners, and connectors occurred in Mexico, and under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3), each foreign component satisfied the required tariff shift of 'a change to heading 8537 from any other heading' in Mexico.

Ruling N303603 evaluates the assembly of electrical junction boxes (subheading 8537.10) in Canada by populating enclosures with terminal blocks, busbars, cross connectors, and mounting hardware. CBP held the origin to be Canada under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) because all foreign components were classifiable outside heading 8537 and underwent the required tariff shift to heading 8537 during assembly in Canada.

In Ruling N303604, CBP evaluated the assembly of an electrical junction box (subheading 8537.10) populated with terminal blocks, a bus bar, cross connectors, and mounting hardware in Canada. CBP held that the assembly of these foreign components into the junction box in Canada satisfied the 19 CFR 102.20 tariff shift rule (a change to heading 8537 from any other heading), conferring Canada as the country of origin under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3).

CBP did not find that a required tariff shift occurred or that a produced material decided origin under 102.11(a) or (b). Instead, CBP held that the panel failed the tariff shift rule under 102.11(a)(3) because foreign components were already classified in heading 8537, essential character under 102.11(b) was not determinative, and origin was ultimately determined under the residual rule of section 102.11(d)(3) as the last country of production.

Ruling N330771 held that the country of origin of the busbar assemblies is Mexico because the assembly processes occurred in Mexico and satisfied the required tariff shift under 19 CFR 102.20 to heading 8537 from non-8537 foreign materials (flexible electrical connectors and insulating materials).

In Ruling N303599, the assembly of a pushbutton switch inside an enclosure (populating an enclosure with a switch under subheading 8536.50) in Canada did not confer origin under 19 CFR Part 102 because the foreign switch (subheading 8536.50) failed to make the required tariff shift, resulting in CBP determining origin to be France under Section 102.11(d)(1).

Ruling H312745 evaluated country of origin for Section 301 purposes using the traditional substantial transformation test (examining whether assembly was complex and meaningful), rather than applying the 19 CFR Part 102 marking rules, and did not make a determination based on tariff shifts or 102.11.

In Ruling N306640, CBP determined the country of origin of the runner assembly to be China under 19 CFR 102.11(b)(1) based on the essential character imparted by the unfinished runner (consisting of the rough machined castings that were welded and roughly machined in China, classified under subheading 8410.90).

Ruling N307465 found that under 19 CFR 102.11(b) and 102.18, the country of origin of the ball valve is China because its essential character is imparted by the Chinese-origin subassembly body (subheading 8481.90), matching the work and component described in the operation group.

In ruling N308442, CBP determined that under 19 CFR 102.11(b) and 102.18, the country of origin of the finished ball valve is China because its essential character is imparted by the Chinese-origin valve subassembly body.

Ruling N317669 decided the country of origin under the traditional substantial transformation test (name, character, or use) for Section 301 trade remedy purposes, not under the 19 CFR Part 102 rules or Section 102.11 tariff shifts.

Ruling N285519 addresses the production of tool holders of heading 8466 in Canada from Spanish polypropylene holders and German hook material, not the casting, forging, welding, or machining of turbine runners (8410.90), valve subassembly bodies (8481.90), or speed reducer casings. Furthermore, CBP concluded that Canada was indeed the country of origin under 19 CFR 102.11(d)(3), contrary to the claim that CBP held another country.

The claim states that the operation group's work did not make the country where the work was done the origin and that CBP held another country. In Ruling N318162, CBP held that the country of origin was Mexico (the country where the grinding, honing, and processing occurred), directly contradicting the claim. Furthermore, the ruling concerns transmission ball bearings (subheading 8482.10) rather than turbine runner subcomponents, valve bodies, or speed reducer casings.

Ruling N334924 concerns wireline drill rods (subheading 8431.43) processed in Canada from imported steel tubes, rather than turbine runner subcomponents, valve bodies, or speed reducer casings. Furthermore, CBP found that the Canadian manufacturing operations DID confer origin on Canada (under substantial transformation principles), directly contradicting the claim that the country where the work was done was not the country of origin.

Ruling N318162 determined the country of origin under the traditional 'substantial transformation' standard for Section 301 trade remedy purposes, not under the 19 CFR Part 102 marking rules (tariff shift/102.11).

The ruling evaluated the country of origin for trade remedy purposes using the traditional substantial transformation test (name, character, or use), rather than applying the 19 CFR Part 102 marking rules or tariff shift rules under 102.11.

Ruling H312745 analyzes the Section 301 country of origin using the substantial transformation test (name, character, use, and whether assembly is complex and meaningful) rather than the 19 CFR Part 102 tariff shift rules, and it does not involve rough castings under subheading 8410.90 or machining/balancing on such castings.

In Ruling N306640, rough runner castings from China (classified in subheading 8410.90) were imported into Canada or Japan for inspection, final machining, and balancing. CBP determined that these operations did not satisfy the required tariff shift for subheading 8410.90 under 19 CFR 102.20 ('change... from any other heading'), and under 19 CFR 102.11(b) the origin remained China because the unfinished runner imparted the essential character.

The ruling's analysis and determination for Section 301 origin purposes were decided under the traditional substantial transformation test (name, character, or use) rather than the 19 CFR Part 102 marking rules (tariff shift rules).

Origin was determined under 19 CFR 102.11(d)(3) because no tariff shift occurred under 102.11(a) and no single material imparted the essential character under 102.11(b), so neither a required tariff shift nor a material deciding origin under 102.11 was present.

Ruling N303499 involves the production of air cylinders classified under subheading 8412.31 in Mexico. Under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3), CBP determined that the components undergo the required tariff shift to subheading 8412.31 in Mexico, making Mexico the country of origin.

The ruling's analysis and determination for Section 301 country of origin were decided under the traditional substantial transformation test (change in name, character, and use), rather than the 19 CFR Part 102 tariff shift rules.

In Ruling N307465, CBP determined that the ball valve (heading 8481) assembly did not satisfy the tariff shift rule under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) because it resulted from a simple assembly, and under 19 CFR 102.11(b), the Chinese origin subassembly body imparted the essential character, deciding origin as China.

In Ruling N308442, assembly of a ball valve (heading 8481) did not confer origin under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) because the tariff shift resulted from a simple assembly. Origin was instead determined under 102.11(b) based on the Chinese origin subassembly body that imparted the essential character.
Ruling N317669 determined country of origin for Section 301 trade remedies using the traditional substantial transformation test (name, character, or use), not the 19 CFR Part 102 tariff shift rules.

The claim asserts that CBP held another country to be the country of origin because the work did not result in origin in the country of processing. However, in Ruling N318162, CBP specifically held that the country of origin was Mexico (the country where the processing took place).

The ruling states that raw cane sugar imported from Brazil is further refined in Canada, meaning the refining of the sugar did not take place in Brazil (the held country of origin). Furthermore, the ruling does not describe processing cocoa beans or milk products in Brazil.

Ruling N322844 held that the country of origin of the SCB 199 Blend is Mexico. The cane sugar in the blend is grown and refined in Mexico (which falls under refining raw cane sugar into white or granulated sugar). Under CBP's 19 CFR Part 102 analysis, foreign cocoa powder was disregarded as de minimis under 102.13, leaving the Mexican-origin sugar as the only ingredient considered, which determined the country of origin of the good to be Mexico.

The operation of refining raw cane sugar took place in Canada, not Brazil or Guatemala (the countries CBP held to be the origin). CBP determined the origin was Brazil, Guatemala, and other Central American countries under 19 CFR 102.11(b) because the raw cane sugar originated there and imparted the essential character, rather than because refining or processing took place in those countries.

The refining of the raw cane sugar occurred in Canada, but CBP held that the countries of origin for marking purposes were Brazil, Guatemala, and the Central American countries (where the raw sugar originated), not Canada. Therefore, the operation group's work was not performed in the country CBP held to be the origin.

The ruling held the country of origin to be Brazil because the raw cane sugar originated in Brazil and imparted the essential character under 102.11(b), whereas the operation group's work (granulating, diluting with water, heating, and filtering into liquid sugar) was performed in Canada and did not effect a qualifying tariff shift or confer origin.

In Ruling N325637, granulated sugar (heading 1701) was produced in Brazil (or Colombia) and served as the essential-character-imparting material under 19 CFR 102.11(b) that determined the country of origin of the finished fermentation starters.

The claim states that the operation group's work or output did not make the country where the work was done the origin and that CBP held another country. However, CBP held that the country of origin was Canada, which is precisely the country where the refining and blending operations took place, because the tariff shift requirements of 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) were satisfied there.

In Ruling N317341, CBP concluded that the country of origin for marking purposes under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) was Canada, not another country. The required tariff shift under Section 102.20 was met in Canada, contradicting the claim that the work did not confer origin or that CBP held another country to be the origin.

In Ruling N320159, CBP held that the country of origin of the product was Canada under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3) because the foreign ingredients (including Brazilian sugar) successfully satisfied the required tariff shift. The claim states that the work did not make the country where it was done the origin and that CBP held another country, which contradicts the ruling's holding.

In Ruling N326397, CBP found that the tariff shift requirement was met and held that the country of origin was Canada (where the manufacturing occurred), directly contradicting the claim that the work did not make the country where it was done the country of origin.

The ruling held that the country of origin of the piping spools was not Mexico, but rather the countries of origin of the component pipes (Czech Republic, Austria, Romania, Japan, South Korea, and the United States). Furthermore, Mexico was where the spools were assembled, not where the pipes themselves were manufactured.

In Ruling N262359, CBP determined that for the pipe spools without valves assembled in Canada, the origin is China under 19 CFR 102.11(b)(1) because the Chinese-origin seamless steel pipe (heading 7304) imparted the essential character to the good.

The claim states that the operation group's work did not make the country where the work was done the origin and that CBP held another country. In Ruling N293362, the work was performed in Mexico, and CBP expressly held that the country of origin is Mexico under Section 102.19 (NAFTA Preference Override).

The claim states that the country where the work was done was not made the origin (i.e. CBP held another country). However, in Ruling N296289, the assembly/processing was performed in Mexico, and CBP expressly held that the country of origin is Mexico pursuant to the NAFTA Preference Override under 19 CFR 102.19.

The claim states that the operation group's work did not make the country where the work was done the origin. However, in Ruling N309421, the manufacturing of tool joints and assembly into drill string assemblies in Mexico did satisfy the tariff shift requirement under 19 CFR 102.11(a)(3), and CBP held that the country of origin was indeed Mexico.

Ruling H312745 evaluated country of origin for Section 301 purposes using the traditional substantial transformation test (change in name, character, and use), rather than applying the 19 CFR Part 102 marking rules (tariff shift or 102.11 essential character analysis).

Ruling N306640 evaluated a hydro-turbine runner assembly where the castings for subcomponents were procured from a Chinese foundry, welded, and rough-machined in China before being sent to Canada/Japan for final processing. CBP determined that the tariff shift rule for subheading 8410.90 was not met in Canada/Japan, and pursuant to 19 CFR 102.11(b) and 102.18(b)(1), the essential character was imparted by the unfinished runner from China (which was already in 8410.90), making China the country of origin.

In ruling N307465, CBP determined under 19 CFR 102.11(b) and 102.18 that the essential character of the ball valve is imparted by the Chinese-origin subassembly body (classified under subheading 8481.90), thereby holding China to be the country of origin.

In Ruling N308442, CBP determined the country of origin under 19 CFR 102.11(b) based on the Chinese-origin subassembly body (classified in subheading 8481.90), which imparts the essential character of the ball valve.

The ruling applied the traditional substantial transformation test for Section 301 origin rather than deciding origin under the 19 CFR Part 102 rules or finding that a required tariff shift or 102.11 analysis took place in China.

The claim asserts that the country where the work was done was not the country of origin because CBP held another country. However, in Ruling N285519, the processing took place in Canada and CBP held that the country of origin is Canada pursuant to 19 CFR 102.11(d)(3).

In Ruling N318162, CBP concluded that performing final grinding and honing in Mexico substantially transformed the rings into precision raceways/races and held that the country of origin was indeed Mexico, directly contradicting the claim that the work did not confer origin on the country where it was done.

In Ruling N334924, the processing (annealing and threading of raw steel tubing into drill rods) performed in Canada was held to confer country of origin on Canada via substantial transformation, directly contradicting the claim that the country where the work was done was not made the country of origin.
